reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
clinicalPearls: A CNS WHO grade 1 intraventricular tumour that in children favours the lateral ventricles and in adults the fourth ventricle.
Hydrocephalus is the dominant clinical problem, arising from cerebrospinal fluid overproduction, obstruction of flow, or impaired reabsorption after microhaemorrhage.
Imaging shows a well-defined, lobulated, avidly and homogeneously enhancing intraventricular mass with a cauliflower-like surface.
Histology recapitulates normal choroid plexus, with delicate fibrovascular fronds lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelium.
Tumour cells commonly express transthyretin and cytokeratins, helping distinguish them from metastatic papillary carcinoma.
It forms a spectrum with atypical papilloma (grade 2) and choroid plexus carcinoma (grade 3), graded largely on mitotic activity and anaplasia.
Choroid plexus tumours, especially carcinoma, are associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome and germline TP53 mutation, and papilloma may occur in Aicardi syndrome.
Complete surgical resection is usually curative for papilloma and often resolves the hydrocephalus.
reference.pathophysiology: Choroid plexus papilloma is a benign neoplasm derived from the modified ependymal epithelium of the choroid plexus, and it faithfully reproduces the papillary architecture of normal plexus with fibrovascular cores covered by a single orderly layer of epithelium. Hydrocephalus results from a combination of active cerebrospinal fluid oversecretion by the expanded epithelial surface, mechanical obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid pathways, and reduced arachnoid reabsorption following recurrent microhaemorrhage that raises fluid protein content. A subset arises in the setting of germline TP53 mutation, linking the choroid plexus tumour spectrum to Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and progression to atypical papilloma and carcinoma is accompanied by increasing mitotic activity, cellular anaplasia and loss of the orderly papillary pattern.
additionalDifferentials: villous hypertrophy of the choroid plexus
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showing an enhancing intraventricular mass
MRI of the whole neuraxis to assess cerebrospinal fluid dissemination
assessment of cerebrospinal fluid dynamics and ventricular size
germline TP53 testing where carcinoma or a suggestive family history is present
developmental and ophthalmological assessment when Aicardi syndrome is suspected
redFlags: rapidly progressive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure
macrocephaly and bulging fontanelle in an infant
features suggesting carcinoma such as brain invasion or dissemination
reference.prognosis: Papilloma carries an excellent prognosis with prolonged survival and frequent cure after complete resection, in marked contrast to choroid plexus carcinoma, which behaves aggressively.
pitfalls: assuming hydrocephalus will always resolve after resection when a shunt may still be needed
misgrading a carcinoma as a benign papilloma on limited sampling
confusing the tumour with reactive villous hypertrophy or normal plexus
overlooking an underlying Li-Fraumeni syndrome and the need for family counselling
underestimating intraoperative bleeding from these vascular tumours
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis et al., cIMPACT-NOW updates on CNS tumour classification
management: Achieve cure with complete surgical resection, the definitive treatment, planning for the tumour's vascularity to limit intraoperative haemorrhage
Treat hydrocephalus, which often resolves after tumour removal but may require cerebrospinal fluid diversion with a shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy
Obtain histological grading to distinguish benign papilloma from atypical papilloma and carcinoma and guide the need for further therapy
Undertake surveillance MRI of the brain, with neuraxis imaging where dissemination is a concern, to detect recurrence
Arrange germline TP53 testing and genetic counselling where the histology or family history is suggestive of Li-Fraumeni syndrome
Follow up through a neurosurgical multidisciplinary team with management of raised intracranial pressure symptoms
